about: The speaking script of the CA talk, one entry per slide of the deck as Kerk rearranged it on 16 November (24 slides: the live demo is slide 2, Bao's slides are 1 to 14, Kerk's are 15 to 23; B1 to B4 are the backup file). 'ref' is the slide's number in the earlier order, used for the folded reference blocks. write_notes.py writes the script into the speaker notes; make_script_docs.py writes it into the master script and the cheat sheet. Plain spoken English: short sentences, one idea at a time. Paragraphs that start with 'Bao:' or 'Kerk:' say who speaks on a shared slide.

We are rebuilding VisuAlgo, and we keep its purpose: helping people learn and explore data structures and algorithms.
Before the slides, let us show you the product. Then I will explain why and how we built it, and Kerk will cover the design process, the engine and the website.

2.message: A tour of the product: familiar home page, one editor for many algorithms, and a run that explains itself in three places.
points: Home page: the same structure as the original VisuAlgo, one card per topic

Planned for the editors: text, free drawing and vertex colours; for lecturers and tutors who teach, and students who draft competitive programming problems; these frequent users, who like to customise, are who the editors are for
Running Dijkstra: the pseudocode line, the Status sentence and a note on the canvas change together; hover shows a shortest path
Tree Editor: LCA with Binary Lifting is a topic I added; the root can be moved
script: This is the running app, not a recording. We start on the home page. Its structure is close to the original VisuAlgo: one card for each topic, so a student can pick a topic and start. Cards marked 'Coming soon' are not rebuilt yet.

What is new are these two editors: the Graph Editor and the Tree Editor. In the Graph Editor, many algorithms live in one place and share one input. This menu lists the eleven graph algorithms we have now. I can also search: I type 'dij', and I get Dijkstra.

Every page has the same parts. On the left is Action, where you choose the input and the options. Next to it is the e-Lecture, which explains the topic. On the right are the pseudocode and Status, which describes the current step. In the middle is the canvas. We call this layout V10, and Kerk will explain later how we arrived at it.

Now let me draw. I drag a vertex to move it. I add a node. I draw an edge from F to the new node, directly on the canvas. The edge also appears in the text on the left, and there I give it a weight of 3. The canvas and the text are two views of the same graph.

Later, we plan to add more tools here, such as text, free drawing and colouring vertices. The aim is that a lecturer or tutor can use the editor to teach, and a student doing competitive programming can use it as a draft, to think through a problem. These frequent users are the people I built the two editors for. They like to set things up their own way.

Now I run Dijkstra from A, one step at a time. Watch three places. The pseudocode highlights the current line. Status explains the step in one sentence. And on the canvas, a short note appears beside the node: zero plus four equals four, so B gets distance 4.
Let me play the rest. At the end, the shortest paths are drawn in green. When I hover a vertex, I see its path: the new node is reached through C, D and F, with distance 8.

Finally, a quick look at the Tree Editor. It works the same way: one tree, shared by Binary Lifting, BST and AVL. Binary Lifting answers lowest common ancestor queries. LCA is an important topic for tree problems, and it is one of the algorithms I added. The tree is easy to edit too. For example, I move the root from 8 to 12, and the same edges are drawn again under the new root.

3.message: We keep VisuAlgo's strengths, and we follow Prof. Halim's directions: better interaction and a wider range of algorithms.
points: VisuAlgo already has custom input and step-by-step runs; we keep them
Prof. Halim's directions: easier graph editing, clearer parallel and curved edges, richer canvas interaction, side-by-side sorting
He also encouraged a wider range of algorithms; LCA and Trie are topics I added
My own focus, from competitive programming and teaching: explain why a step happens
script: VisuAlgo already lets students try their own inputs and follow an algorithm step by step. We want to keep these strengths.

In our early meetings, Prof. Halim suggested several directions. First, easier graph editing, with clearer parallel and curved edges. Second, richer interaction on the canvas. Third, comparing sorting algorithms side by side. He also encouraged us to cover a wider range of algorithms. The two examples on the last card, LCA and Trie, are topics I added.
These directions were our starting point, and the prototypes helped us explore them.
I come from competitive programming and teaching, so I care about one more thing. Students should understand why a step happens, not only see the final answer.

4.message: In the original code, one common change touches several topics, so we reorganised the foundation.
points: The platform grew over many years; some parts are shared, such as the graph widget
But each topic has its own input handling and state building
So one editing change means changes and checks in several topics
Sorting comparison: each pane needs its own state, with shared controls
Decision: reorganise the foundation, and keep tools that fit, such as D3
script: The original platform has grown over many years, with many contributors. It already shares some parts, such as the graph widget in this diagram.

But a lot of logic still lives inside each topic. In the graph modules we looked at, each topic handles its own input and builds its own visual state. So one change to graph editing means changes and checks in several topics.
Sorting comparison raises a different problem. Each pane needs its own state, but one set of controls must drive all of them. Splitting the screen is not enough.
So we decided to reorganise the foundation. We chose boundaries that support these interactions, and we keep useful tools, such as D3, where they fit.

script: These early prototypes were experiments toward the goals we discussed with Prof. Halim. Each one tested a different requirement.

Start with Graph, on the left. My first prototype had separate views for editing and running. In the rewrite, I kept one canvas, and I separated the input, the positions and the playback. So a learner can move a vertex and stay on the same step of the algorithm.

One note on names. This standalone Graph rewrite is not the layout we later call V2. I will keep the two names apart.

So the interaction stays consistent, because each piece of state has one clear owner.

script: Binary Lifting is one of the topics I added. A query has several stages, and it reads an ancestor table.

[Press → to play the clip.] I move the root from 10 to 16. Then I ask for the LCA of 8 and 20. 8 is deeper, so it lifts two levels, to 4. Now both ancestors are 16, so u and v stay. At k = 0, the ancestors 10 and 18 differ, so both lift. Their parent, 16, is the answer.

Notice what happened. During the query, no node moved. And five of the twelve steps only decided to stay: two while 8 was catching up, and three at ancestor 16. Without a note, those steps look the same.
With floating text, the reason sits beside the node. The learner can read it without leaving the tree. Status still keeps the full sentence.
I added this after the Week 10 trial. As I remember it, newer learners often had to read Status for algorithms with several stages, such as LCA. We have not yet measured whether floating text helps.
The same rooted tree and ancestor queries also prepare the ground for more advanced tree topics later.

script: This is the architecture of the system. On the left is the browser, on the right the server.

In the browser, the frontend holds the React interface: the design tokens, the panels and the e-Lectures. It starts a run in the algorithm engine, which is C++ compiled to WebAssembly. The engine records a history, and the render engine draws that history.

On the server, a Go API handles accounts, preferences and progress. It uses Postgres for users, progress and content, Redis for login sessions and cache, and an email provider for login and reset codes.

One thing must be clear. The demo you saw runs TypeScript algorithms in the browser. The algorithm engine in this diagram is not connected to those visualizers yet. Connecting them is Semester 2 work.

script: The engine foundation explores running C++ algorithms, compiled to WebAssembly, inside a worker.

The page and the engine talk through protocol messages, not through direct calls into the visual components. The worker gives execution its own context. The page stays responsible for interaction and drawing.
The documented engine uses protobuf messages, with graph and array representations. It also has a Python path, through Pyodide, for tracing sorting algorithms.
The main design question is this. How do we expose enough state for visualization, without making the engine depend on the page layout?

Our answer is a division of work. The engine should describe the algorithm's state and its changes. The visualizer still has to explain them to the learner. For example, when the engine updates a distance, it does not decide where a note appears, or which pseudocode line to highlight. That belongs to the integration boundary.

script: The engine and the visualizers keep history in different ways.

The documented engine keeps a reversible journal: a record for each step, and it can move backward through those records. The current Graph and Tree visualizers build all their steps when a run starts. Sorting pulls operations from generators and keeps history for seeking.
So connecting them needs an explicit translation. We cannot simply replace one algorithm function with another.

Three things must stay consistent. First, the identity of nodes and edges, especially parallel edges. Second, the identity of a run, when the user changes the input or starts again. Third, the meaning of a step: the drawing, the pseudocode and the text must agree.
Bao did an earlier integration experiment, with stable edge identities and a browser client. It remains separate from the delivered visualizers.
Our proposed next step is one complete Graph integration, checked against the current TypeScript behaviour, before we expand.

script: The website has to host the visualizers without duplicating their controls.

In the prototype, the site owns the top bar and the theme. Each visualizer supplies the topic-specific parts, such as the algorithm choices or the sorting pane controls. The host then presents them inside one site.

Bao built the working catalogue, the routes and the host adapters, on top of the design system. My consolidation and refinements made it a single application. So this boundary is where our contributions meet.
The wider website infrastructure and the engine still need to come together with the visualization layer.
Keeping these responsibilities explicit helps us avoid two problems: a second set of playback controls, and conflicting theme state.

To finish, our plan for Semester 2. Our next integration milestone is one Graph algorithm working across the full application. The input, the engine and the playback must agree on three things: node and edge identity, the meaning of each step, and cancellation. We can check the result against the current TypeScript version before we go further.
We are targeting a first public release around March 2027, depending on integration and validation. The current plan keeps the original platform available, and links to the completed topics.

Bao will stabilise the workflows you saw today and evaluate the new explanations with defined tasks. Our wider ambition is to cover the original range of algorithms and, later, to add advanced tree topics, such as Heavy-Light Decomposition or Centroid Decomposition. These are possibilities, not Semester 2 commitments. Integration, validation and stability come first.
